temporize.definition: to delay in order to gain time
sentences: He temporized for three weeks and the decision made itself.
Temporizing is a strategy right up until somebody else acts.

tenable.definition: able to be defended or maintained
sentences: The position was tenable until the third dataset arrived.
A tenable theory is one that could in principle be wrong and is not.
A tenacious local campaign saved the line that four studies had condemned.
Tenacious mud on the boots outlasted three washes.
Her tenacity over eleven years achieved what talent alone would not have.
Tenacity is admired in a rival and exhausting in a housemate.
The tendentious summary quoted every supporting line and none of the caveats.
A tendentious question shapes the answer before it is asked.
He tendered his resignation on Friday and withdrew it on Monday.
Four firms tendered for the contract and the cheapest one collapsed midway.
A tentative conclusion in the abstract became a certainty in the press release.
His tentative knock was answered only on the third attempt.
The connection between the two events is tenuous and was reported as causal.
Her grip on the department was tenuous and held for nine more years.
A tepid endorsement from her own department killed the application.
The tepid coffee had been made, apparently, during the previous session.

terrestrial.definition: relating to the earth or land
sentences: Terrestrial broadcasting survived satellite and streaming and one attempt to abolish it.
Terrestrial animals evolved from aquatic ones and kept the salt in their blood.

territory.definition: an area of land or sphere of activity
sentences: That question is another department's territory, which is why nobody answered it.
The cat patrolled a territory of four gardens with unshakable confidence.

terse.definition: brief and to the point, sometimes curtly
sentences: The terse reply — "No." — was framed by the recipient.
Terse writing is not rude; terse answers to sincere questions usually are.

testator.definition: a person who has made a will
sentences: The testator's intentions were clear and his handwriting was not.
The testator added a codicil three days before dying, which is always litigated.
In science a theory is the strongest thing available, not a guess.
The theory explains four observations and predicts a fifth that has now been made.

thorough.definition: complete and careful in every detail
sentences: A thorough search found the file in the one box nobody had opened.
Thorough work is invisible; only its absence gets noticed.
The report demanded a thoroughgoing reform and got a working group.
He is a thoroughgoing pessimist and remarkably good company.

thrall.definition: a state of being controlled by something
sentences: The whole field was in thrall to a model nobody had tested in twenty years.
Thrall was the Old Norse word for a slave, which the metaphor still carries.
The threadbare excuse about the printer had been used four times that month.
His threadbare jacket was older than most of his students.
Thrifty habits learned in one bad decade lasted a comfortable lifetime.
Thrifty and stingy differ mainly in who is describing you.
A throng gathered outside the courthouse and dispersed the moment it rained.
The throng at the station made the four-minute connection impossible.
The plan was thwarted by a locked gate that appeared on no map.
She thwarted the takeover by finding one clause in a 1978 agreement.
The tide of opinion turned in a fortnight and nobody could say precisely why.
Time and tide wait for no man, and one of them is at least predictable.
A timely reminder prevented an error that would have cost the quarter.
The intervention was timely by about four hours.
A timorous first question opened a discussion that lasted three hours.
Timorous leadership in a crisis is worse than the wrong decision made confidently.
The tirade lasted eleven minutes and was, unfortunately, being recorded.
A tirade relieves the speaker and persuades nobody.
Surrounded by toadies, he learned about the crisis from the newspaper.
A toady was originally the assistant who pretended to eat a toad in a quack's show.
Years of toil in the archive produced one paragraph that changed the field.
The toil is in the checking; the glory is in the abstract.
A token consultation was held on a Friday afternoon in August.
The token gesture cost eleven pounds and was reported as commitment.
The tome sat on the desk for four years, consulted and never read through.
He wrote a tome where an essay would have been read.
The market was torpid all summer and violent in September.
Torpid after lunch, the committee approved everything on the agenda.

torpor.definition: a state of inactivity and lethargy
sentences: A general torpor settled on the department in the second year of the freeze.
The torpor of hibernation lets a body run at a fraction of normal cost.
Too much torque sheared the bolt and doubled the repair.
Electric motors deliver full torque immediately, which is why they feel so fast.
A torrid week in July emptied the office and filled the parks.
Their torrid dispute in the correspondence pages lasted eleven issues.
The tortuous route through four departments took eight months.
Tortuous is twisting; torturous is painful, and a long meeting can be both.
The tour covered nine cities and one memorable hotel corridor.
A tour of the building revealed everything the brochure had avoided.
The scheme was touted as revolutionary and was, on inspection, a spreadsheet.
He touted his connections and produced none of them when needed.

tract.definition: a pamphlet on a serious subject; an area of land
sentences: The tract was printed in 1723 and answered by nine others within a year.
A tract of moorland the size of a county is owned by four people.
The problem became tractable the moment somebody restated it in two dimensions.
A tractable colleague is pleasant; an entirely tractable one is a warning.
He was traduced in a pamphlet whose author never signed it.
To traduce a rival is easier than to answer them and lasts longer.
The tranquil surface of the reservoir conceals a drowned village.
A tranquil morning was ruined by one email at nine-fifteen.

transcend.definition: to go beyond the limits of
sentences: The performance transcended a script that nobody could defend on the page.
Her work transcends the field it started in, which is why it is taught elsewhere.

transgression.definition: a violation of a rule or law
sentences: The transgression was minor and the cover-up was not.
Every institution defines transgression by what threatens it, not by what harms.
The transient population of the town triples in July and vanishes in September.
A transient fault is the hardest kind to fix and the easiest to blame on the user.
The inflation was declared transitory for four consecutive quarters.
Fame is transitory and the photographs are not.

transmute.definition: to change into a different form
sentences: Grief transmuted, over years, into a foundation that funds research.
Alchemists failed to transmute lead into gold and invented chemistry instead.
He acquired all the trappings of authority and none of the actual power.
The trappings of office cost more to maintain than the office paid.
The travails of the first two years are absent from every profile written since.
After much travail the bridge opened, four years late and beautiful.
The trial was a travesty and its verdict was quoted as precedent for years.
The adaptation was a travesty that its own author refused to watch.
The treacherous path along the cliff has a handrail installed after each accident.
A treacherous ally is more expensive than an honest enemy.
The treacly voiceover undid every honest moment in the documentary.
Treacle is thick, dark syrup, which is exactly what the prose resembles.

tread.definition: to walk or step, often carefully
sentences: He trod carefully around a subject the whole room had agreed to ignore.
Tread softly, wrote Yeats, because you tread on my dreams.
The treatise on drainage runs to nine hundred pages and is still cited.
He replied to a two-line email with a treatise.
A trenchant paragraph in the middle of the review is what everyone quoted.
Trenchant criticism cuts; the useful kind also shows where to cut.

trepidation.definition: fearful anxiety about what may happen
sentences: She opened the review with some trepidation and found four lines of praise.
Trepidation before a first lecture never entirely goes away, which is healthy.
After many tribulations the building opened, three years late and much loved.
The tribulations of the journey filled a diary that his family never read.

tribunal.definition: a body appointed to judge disputes
sentences: The tribunal found for the employee and awarded a sum that changed nothing.
An employment tribunal is cheaper than a court and slower than either party expects.
A trifling sum in the accounts turned out to be the thread that unravelled everything.
They argued for two hours over a trifling difference in wording.
The trite closing line undid an unusually careful argument.
Trite comes from a word meaning worn away by rubbing.
A triumvirate of deputies ran the place for eleven months and agreed on nothing.
Rome's first triumvirate lasted seven years and ended in civil war.
The trivial detail on page nine was the only part anyone could verify.
Trivial in mathematics means true for boring reasons, not unimportant.
He plighted his troth in 1911 and kept it for fifty-four years.
Troth is the same word as truth, worn down by centuries of use.
The truculence of the reply guaranteed a second letter from the regulator.
Truculence in negotiation is usually a sign of a weak position.
A truculent witness made the prosecution's case for it.
He was truculent at the start of every meeting and reasonable by the end.
The report was truncated by four pages and the removed pages contained the caveats.
The database truncated every name at twenty characters, which caused eleven years of confusion.

truncated.definition: shortened by having an end cut off
sentences: A truncated season meant the title was decided by fewer matches than usual.
The truncated pyramid at the site was never finished, not damaged.
In the tumult after the announcement nobody heard the important second sentence.
The tumult of the market at six in the morning is its own kind of order.
A tumultuous decade produced four governments and one lasting reform.
Tumultuous applause greeted a speech that read badly the next morning.
The turbid water made the survey impossible for three days.
His turbid prose obscures an argument that is probably quite good.
A turbulent year for the company ended with the same chief executive, improbably.
Turbulent flow is the point at which the mathematics stops being helpful.

tureen.definition: a deep covered dish for soup
sentences: The tureen has been in the family since 1840 and used, by count, eleven times.
A tureen keeps soup hot and takes up half the table.
The turgid introduction defeated three reviewers before the argument began.
Turgid prose is what happens when nobody dares to edit the senior author.
Visa forms still ask about crimes of moral turpitude, which nobody defines.
The turpitude alleged in the pamphlet turned out to be a parking dispute.
Under her tutelage the department produced four professors in a decade.
Tutelage that lasts too long becomes a cage.
The tyro's question exposed an assumption nobody senior had examined for years.
Every tyro is one embarrassing mistake away from being useful.
The logo became ubiquitous in a year and invisible in the second.
Ubiquitous surveillance is noticed only in the rooms where it is absent.
The generosity had an ulterior motive that emerged four months later.
Ulterior means lying beyond, which is where motives usually are.
He took umbrage at a joke that had not been about him.
Umbrage comes from shade: to take offense is to feel overshadowed.
The unadorned account of the events was more damning than any editorial.
An unadorned white room shows every fingerprint, which is its whole philosophy.
Her unaffected pleasure at the small prize was the best part of the evening.
Unaffected manners are the hardest thing to imitate.
The evening was an unalloyed success, which happens roughly once a decade.
Unalloyed pleasure is rarer than the phrase suggests.
The unanimity of the vote concealed four separate private objections.
Unanimity in a committee usually means the question was too vague.
Her reputation was unassailable until one footnote proved to be invented.
An unassailable lead in October has been lost by April more than once.
The unassuming man at the back of the room had funded the entire building.
Unassuming people are consistently underestimated, which several of them use deliberately.
She had an uncanny knack for predicting which projects would fail.
The uncanny valley is where a robot is almost human and therefore horrifying.
Her uncompromising standards cost the department two contracts and won it a reputation.
Uncompromising in principle and impossible in practice describes most manifestos.
An unconscionable delay of eleven years was described as regrettable.
The contract was struck down as unconscionable, which is a rare judicial verdict.
His uncouth manners at dinner obscured a genuinely first-rate mind.
Uncouth originally meant simply unknown, and rudeness attached itself later.
He delivered the condolences with an unction that made them worse.
Extreme unction is a sacrament; the other kind is a manner.
The unctuous salesman agreed with everything and delivered nothing.
Unctuous literally means oily, which is exactly how the manner feels.

undercut.definition: to weaken or offer at a lower price
sentences: His own footnote undercut the argument he had spent forty pages making.
They undercut every competitor for two years and then raised prices.
A steady drip of anonymous comments undermined a manager nobody would confront.
Water undermined the foundations for forty years before the wall moved.
The failure underscored a weakness three previous reports had described politely.
She underscored the deadline three times and it was still missed.
The understated design has outlasted four fashionable ones next to it.
His understated summary of the disaster was more alarming than any shouting.
She undertook to deliver by March and delivered in February.
Nobody undertakes a nine-year project expecting it to take nine years.

undertaking.definition: a formal promise or a large task
sentences: The undertaking was given in writing and honored, remarkably, in full.
Cataloguing the collection was an undertaking that consumed two careers.
A single donor underwrote the season and asked for no credit at all.
The government underwrote the loans and discovered what it had guaranteed in 2009.
A student unearthed the letter in a box marked "miscellaneous."
The excavation unearthed a road that no document had ever mentioned.
The evidence was unequivocal and the denial continued for two more years.
An unequivocal answer in that culture would itself have been the insult.
The statement was unexceptionable and therefore said nothing at all.
Unexceptionable means nobody can object; unexceptional means nobody will notice.
Her unfaltering support during the inquiry was remembered for the rest of his career.
The unfaltering rhythm of the machine was audible three streets away.
Unfettered access to the archive produced four books in six years.
Unfettered markets and unfettered rivers both eventually require embankments.
The unflappable duty manager handled a fire alarm and a lost child simultaneously.
Unflappable is a quality you notice only in the one week it is needed.
The ungainly machine worked flawlessly for thirty years.
His ungainly stride was recognizable from the far end of the corridor.
The source was unimpeachable and, on this occasion, wrong.
Unimpeachable conduct over thirty years was undone by one expense claim.
Universal agreement in the room lasted until the funding was mentioned.
The universal grammar hypothesis has been argued about for sixty years.

unmitigated.definition: absolute; not lessened in any way
sentences: The launch was an unmitigated disaster and a superb learning experience.
Unmitigated praise makes readers suspicious and rightly so.
The silence unnerved him more than any of the questions had.
Nothing unnerves a speaker like an audience taking notes at the wrong moment.
The measure was unprecedented in peacetime and became routine within a year.
"Unprecedented" is used most often by people who have not checked.
The unprepossessing building holds the best collection in the country.
An unprepossessing first chapter has cost many good books their readers.
It was an unpropitious moment to ask for money and he asked anyway.
The unpropitious weather on opening day set the tone for the season.
Unremitting pressure over four years produced a policy change in one afternoon.
The unremitting cheerfulness of the campaign became slightly menacing.
An unruly meeting produced the year's only genuinely new idea.
His unruly hair was mentioned in every profile and in none of the reviews.
An unscrupulous agent charged both parties and represented neither.
Unscrupulous does not mean stupid, which is what makes it dangerous.
There was an unseemly rush for the exit before the final speaker finished.
Unseemly haste in appointing a successor was noted in three obituaries.
The memoir is unsparing about its author, which is rarer than being unsparing about others.
She was unsparing with her time and merciless about wasted meetings.
His unstinting support for junior colleagues is what the department actually remembers.
Unstinting praise from a hard marker is worth four prizes.
Untempered enthusiasm in the first year became untempered cynicism in the third.
Untempered steel is hard and shatters, which is a fair metaphor for people.
His position became untenable the moment the emails were published.
The theory is untenable and continues to appear in undergraduate textbooks.
Nothing untoward was found in the accounts, which surprised at least four people.
An untoward remark at the reception was smoothed over by the host within a minute.
Untrammeled by a brief, the designer produced something nobody could afford.
A trammel was a net or shackle, so untrammeled means genuinely loose.

unwonted.definition: unusual for the person or situation
sentences: He spoke with unwonted warmth about a colleague he usually described as adequate.
Unwonted means unaccustomed; unwanted means something else entirely.
She upbraided the committee for a decision it had not actually made.
He upbraided himself for a fortnight over an email nobody remembered.
The upshot of eleven months of consultation was a car park.
The upshot is that nothing changed and everybody is now very tired.
His urbane manner disguised an upbringing he never discussed.
Urbane comes from the city, which is where the manners were supposed to be.
The committee usurped a function it had been created to advise on.
He usurped the role gradually, one meeting at a time.
Usury was forbidden for centuries and practiced continuously under other names.
What counts as usury has moved with every change in the base rate.

utilitarian.definition: designed for use rather than beauty
sentences: The utilitarian building outlasted the beautiful one next to it by forty years.
Utilitarian ethics counts consequences, which sounds simple and never is.
The plan was utter nonsense and was implemented in full.
There was utter silence for four seconds, which felt considerably longer.
The instructions were utterly clear and universally ignored.
He was utterly certain and, as the recording showed, utterly wrong.

vacate.definition: to leave a place or position empty
sentences: They vacated the building on Friday and the lease ran for another two years.
The court vacated the judgment, which sent everyone back to the beginning.
He vacillated for a month and lost both options.
Vacillating publicly is worse than deciding wrongly and explaining why.
The vacuous slogan was tested with focus groups and survived them all.
A vacuous smile at the wrong moment can end an interview.
The vagaries of the funding cycle decided which questions got asked.
The vagaries of English spelling defeat native speakers daily.
A vain attempt to save the building lasted nine years and one appeal.
He was vain about his hair and modest about everything that mattered.
The vainglorious memoir mentions his colleagues twice in four hundred pages.
Vainglory is pride that insists on an audience.
The medal for valor was awarded to a cook who drove the ambulance.
Discretion is the better part of valor, said the character pretending to be dead.

vanguard.definition: the leading position in a movement
sentences: The lab was in the vanguard for a decade and a museum by the next one.
The vanguard is the most exposed position, which is why it changes hands often.
The champion was vanquished by an opponent ranked ninety-fourth.
He vanquished his fear of flying by taking eleven short flights in a fortnight.
The vapid interview questions produced vapid answers, to nobody's surprise.
Vapid originally described drink that had lost its flavor.
His account was at variance with the security log by ninety minutes.
The variance in the results was larger than the effect being measured.
The variegated leaves are a mutation that gardeners have carefully preserved.
A variegated career of nine jobs looked, in the obituary, like a plan.

vassal.definition: a subordinate dependent on a superior
sentences: The smaller state was a vassal in everything but the wording of the treaty.
A vassal owed service and received protection, which was the whole arrangement.
The vat holds four thousand liters and takes two days to clean.
Somebody fell into the dye vat in 1908 and the story improves annually.
The vaunted new system failed in its first week of actual use.
Their vaunted defense conceded four goals in twenty minutes.
His vehement denial was longer and less convincing than a short one would have been.
Vehement opposition from four residents delayed the scheme for six years.
A venal inspector signed off on a building that collapsed within a decade.
Venal means bribable; venial means forgivable, and confusing them changes everything.
The venality of the licensing office was an open secret for twenty years.
Venality is cheaper to buy than incompetence is to fix.
A veneer of consultation covered a decision made in February.
The veneer is walnut and the carcass is chipboard, which the auctioneer omitted.

venerable.definition: commanding respect through age or achievement
sentences: The venerable institution changed its rules for the first time since 1911.
Venerable is a compliment that also means old, which recipients notice.
The founder is venerated in the annual report and ignored in the practice.
Cultures that venerate their elders still argue with them at dinner.
The venerated text turned out to be a nineteenth-century compilation.
A venerated colleague can be the hardest person to correct.
A venial error in the footnotes was treated as though it were fraud.
Venial sins are forgivable; mortal ones are not, in the theology that invented both.

venture.definition: to risk saying or doing something
sentences: She ventured an opinion that turned out to be the only correct one.
Nothing ventured, nothing gained, said the man who lost the deposit.
The veracious account was duller and considerably more useful than the dramatic one.
Veracious means truthful; voracious means hungry, and the difference matters.
The veracity of the witness was tested by a parking receipt.
Nobody questioned his veracity, only his memory.
The verbose contract hid three important clauses in a fog of ordinary ones.
Verbose writing is usually a first draft that nobody finished.
The verdant valley in the brochure is verdant for about six weeks a year.
After the rains the hillside turned verdant almost overnight.
The forgery was verisimilar in every detail except the watermark.
A verisimilar account is not the same as a true one, which is the whole problem.
The novel's verisimilitude comes from four years of the author working the job.
Verisimilitude in fiction requires more research than truth does in journalism.
The attic held a veritable museum of things nobody had needed since 1974.
A veritable flood of applications arrived on the final afternoon.
The vernal equinox is when day and night are, briefly, equal.
A vernal enthusiasm for the new project lasted until the first frost.

versatile.definition: able to adapt to many functions
sentences: The versatile little tool has stayed in the drawer for thirty years and earned it.
A versatile player covers four positions and is picked for none of them.
She played with a verve that the recording never quite captures.
The essay has verve and no evidence, which describes most opinion columns.
A vestige of the old railway survives as a footpath and a very straight hedge.
Not a vestige of the argument remained by the following morning.
The vestments in the cathedral museum are embroidered with a gold thread nobody can now source.
He wore the vestments of authority and exercised none of it.
The question has vexed the field for eighty years and remains open.
It vexed him that the correction never traveled as far as the error.

vexation.definition: annoyance or a cause of it
sentences: The chief vexation of the job was a photocopier with opinions.
To his evident vexation, the intern's version was better.
The business was viable for eleven months and never once profitable.
A viable alternative existed and was rejected for arriving in the wrong format.
He took vicarious pleasure in a career he had talked his son out of.
Vicarious liability makes the employer answer for the employee's mistake.
The vicissitudes of the funding cycle shaped every research question asked.
Through all the vicissitudes of a long career she kept the same desk.
Four candidates vied for a post that was abolished within a year.
The two theories vied for a decade and were both replaced by a third.
A vigilant neighbor noticed the smoke nine minutes before the alarm did.
Being vigilant for years without incident is the hardest kind of work.
He pursued the correction with a vigor the original error had never received.
The plant regained its vigor after a hard pruning everyone had opposed.
She was vilified for a decade and honored in the eleventh year.
It is easier to vilify a person than to refute their argument.
She tackled the accounts with a vim that alarmed the finance office.
Vim and vigor is a phrase used exclusively by people over seventy.

vindicate.definition: to clear of blame or prove right
sentences: The findings vindicated a position she had held alone for nine years.
He was vindicated by an inquiry that nobody read.
The vindictive footnote named a rival who had died four years earlier.
Vindictive management produces obedient staff and no information.

vintage.definition: of high quality from an earlier period
sentences: That reply was vintage him: three words and no room for argument.
Vintage originally referred to the year a wine was harvested.
The vintner recommended the cheapest bottle on the list, which is how trust is built.
Four generations of vintners farmed a slope the size of two tennis courts.
History calls her a virago; the letters show a woman running an estate alone.
Virago originally meant a heroic woman, which is how far the word has fallen.

virtual.definition: in effect though not formally so
sentences: He had virtual control of the company through a shareholding of eleven percent.
A virtual monopoly is a monopoly with better lawyers.
The virtuoso played the impossible passage twice and complained about the piano.
A virtuoso performance in a bad production is a strange kind of waste.
The virulent strain spread through the ward before anyone identified it.
His virulent attack on the paper cost him more than the paper.
His stern visage in the portrait is contradicted by every letter he wrote.
The visage on the coin belongs to a man nobody has otherwise recorded.
The viscid resin trapped an insect that is now ninety million years old.
The mixture turns viscid at exactly the temperature the recipe fails to mention.
The oil is too viscous for the pump in January and fine by April.
Glass is often called a very viscous liquid, which physicists dispute annually.
The visionary plan of 1962 was implemented, in a diminished form, in 1998.
Visionary is what we call an obsessive whose idea worked.
The market's vitality at six in the morning shames every office in the city.
Vitality returned to the department when the funding did.
One undisclosed conflict of interest vitiated the entire report.
A single false premise vitiates an otherwise flawless argument.
The vitriol in the comment section outlasted the article by four years.
Vitriol is literally sulfuric acid, which the metaphor takes seriously.
The vitriolic review was written, it later emerged, by a rejected applicant.
A vitriolic exchange in the letters page ran for eleven weeks.
He vituperated against the committee in language the minutes could not record.
Vituperating a rival makes excellent copy and poor argument.
The vivacious host kept a difficult table talking for four hours.
Vivacious in company and silent on paper describes a great many people.

vociferous.definition: loud and insistent in expressing views
sentences: A vociferous minority delayed the plan by four years and improved it slightly.
The most vociferous objector became the loudest defender within a year.

volatile.definition: unstable and liable to change suddenly
sentences: The volatile market moved eleven percent in a week and finished where it started.
A volatile temperament is exhausting for everyone except biographers.

volubility.definition: the quality of talking fluently and at length
sentences: His volubility in interviews contrasted with a lifetime of unanswered letters.
The volubility of the witness worked against her in the transcript.
The voluble guide covered nine centuries and one very long anecdote about a goat.
Voluble on his subject and monosyllabic on everything else.

voracious.definition: having a huge appetite, literal or figurative
sentences: A voracious reader, she finished four books on the flight and started a fifth.
Voracious means hungry; veracious means truthful, and the two get swapped constantly.

waffle.definition: to talk or write vaguely at length
sentences: He waffled for four minutes rather than admit he had not read it.
The essay waffles for two pages and makes its point in the third.

waft.definition: to drift gently through the air
sentences: The smell of baking wafted up the stairwell and emptied four offices.
Snow wafted past the window without ever quite arriving.

waive.definition: to give up a right or requirement
sentences: The fee was waived for anyone who asked, which almost nobody did.
He waived his right to appeal in exchange for a shorter sentence.
A wan smile was the only response the joke deserved.
He looked wan after the flight and recovered entirely over dinner.

wander.definition: to move without a fixed course
sentences: His attention wandered in the fourth hour and never returned.
They wandered the old quarter for an afternoon and found the best meal of the trip.
Interest waned in the second year and the funding followed in the third.
The moon waxes and wanes and gives English two useful verbs.
The security arrangements were found wanting on the one night they mattered.
Weighed in the balance and found wanting is a very old and very effective phrase.
Wanton destruction of the orchard was described in court as high spirits.
Wanton disregard for the rules is a legal phrase and an accurate one.
A blackbird warbled from the chimney at four in the morning, daily, for a month.
He warbled his way through the anthem and the crowd forgave him.
The evidence does not warrant the confidence of the conclusion.
The delay warranted an explanation and received an apology instead.
The criticism was warranted and the manner of delivering it was not.
A warranted intervention is easier to defend afterward than a lucky one.
Be wary of a forecast that has never once been wrong.
He was wary of the offer and accepted a worse one from someone he knew.
She never wavered in public and rewrote the decision four times in private.
The flame wavered and the whole room held its breath.

wax.definition: to increase; to speak at length
sentences: Enthusiasm waxed through the autumn and waned by February.
He waxed lyrical about the coastline for twenty minutes.
She was waylaid in the corridor by three people with the same question.
He waylaid the minister between the lift and the car and got his answer.
The wayward son of the family founded the business that saved it.
A wayward shot in the ninetieth minute decided the whole season.
Weary of the argument, she conceded a point she had won three times.
The weary traveler slept through the station she had been awake for.

weather.definition: to come safely through a difficulty
sentences: The firm weathered the crisis by selling the building it had just bought.
Weathered stone is more beautiful and structurally worse than fresh.
He weighed the options for a month and chose the first one.
Weigh the evidence before deciding whose account to believe.

welt.definition: a raised mark on the skin
sentences: The welt across his forearm was from a branch and not, as everyone assumed, a fight.
A welt in shoemaking is the strip that joins the upper to the sole.
A welter of conflicting instructions arrived from four different offices.
In the welter of data one clean series told the whole story.
He wheedled an extension out of a lecturer known for granting none.
Children learn to wheedle before they learn to argue, which is efficient.
The first chapter whets the appetite and the second one satisfies it entirely.
A whetstone sharpens the blade, which is where the metaphor comes from.
The whimsical illustrations undercut a text that was entirely serious.
A whimsical decision about the office layout produced four years of complaint.
The internal review whitewashed the incident and was itself later reviewed.
Whitewashing a wall hides the damp for one summer.
The shortlist was whittled from ninety to four over eleven weeks.
He whittled the stick into something and could never say what.
The whorls of a fingerprint form before birth and never change.
Whorls in the wood grain show where a branch once was.
Willful ignorance of the warnings was the finding of the whole report.
A willful child and a determined adult are the same person at different ages.
The wily old negotiator conceded first and gained everything afterward.
Wily competitors do not announce what they are doing.

winnow.definition: to sift out the valuable from the worthless
sentences: They winnowed four hundred applications down to nine over a fortnight.
Winnowing separates grain from chaff by throwing both into the wind.
Her winsome delivery made a dull subject genuinely watchable.
Winsome comes from an Old English word for joy, which the word still carries.
He grew wistful about a job he had complained about daily for nine years.
A wistful glance at the old building is the last thing every alumnus does.
The wizened apple in the bowl had been there since the previous autumn.
A wizened figure in the corner turned out to be the founder.
A woeful lack of preparation was concealed by a very good slide deck.
Their woeful record that season made the eventual promotion inexplicable.
As was his wont, he arrived nine minutes late and apologized to nobody.
Wont is habit; won't is refusal, and the apostrophe does all the work.
A wraith of steam rose from the pavement after the rain.
He came back from the illness a wraith and was himself again by spring.

wrangle.definition: to argue noisily and at length
sentences: They wrangled over the wording for eleven weeks and published unchanged.
The legal wrangle outlasted both original parties.
The storm wreaked havoc on a coastline that had just been repaired.
Wreak havoc is nearly the only surviving use of a once-common verb.
A wry footnote in the appendix is the only joke in four hundred pages.
He gave a wry smile at a compliment he knew to be undeserved.
The campaign's xenophobia was denied by everyone who had written it.
Xenophobia rises with insecurity more reliably than with immigration.
The xenophobic pamphlet was printed abroad, which nobody found funny at the time.
Xenophobic policies are usually announced as practical measures.
She did yeoman work on the index that nobody thanked her for.
A yeoman was a small landowner, which is where the reliability comes from.
The archive yielded nothing for four months and everything in one afternoon.
He yielded the point and won the argument twenty minutes later.

yoke.definition: a burden of oppression or servitude
sentences: They threw off the yoke of one authority and accepted another within a decade.
A yoke joins two oxen so neither can pull away, which is the metaphor exactly.

zeal.definition: great energy in pursuit of a cause
sentences: His zeal for the reform exceeded his understanding of what it required.
Zeal without knowledge, says the proverb, is a runaway horse.
The zealots on both sides made the compromise impossible and inevitable.
A zealot is somebody who cannot change their mind and will not change the subject.
A zealous new inspector found eleven violations that four predecessors had walked past.
Zealous enforcement of a bad rule is worse than the rule.

zeitgeist.definition: the defining spirit of a period
sentences: The book caught the zeitgeist so exactly that it is now unreadable.
Zeitgeist is German for time-spirit and has no shorter English equivalent.
The company reached its zenith in 1998 and nobody noticed until 2003.
Zenith is directly overhead; nadir is directly below.
A zephyr through the open window was the only relief all afternoon.
Zephyrus was the Greek west wind, the mildest of the four.
